newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS - Russia oil tariff cut not set to lift exports.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Russia oil tariff cut not set to lift exports.

text.p: Russian producers will probably try to squeeze a few extra barrels of oil through export routes, if the Federal Energy Commission (FEC) succeeds in a bid to slash pipeline tariffs in May, industry sources said on Thursday.
But the scope for higher deliveries to world markets through an already overcrowded export pipeline system is strictly limited, they said.

"Tariff cuts would make it more profitable to export, so oil companies will certainly try to export as much as they can," said Stuart Amor, energy analyst at CS First Boston in London. "But the export pipelines are already basically full."
The FEC said it planned to reduce oil and oil product transport tariffs by 20 percent in May, in a move which would help Russian oil producers increase profitability.
Pavel Serikov, head of the group's price regulation section, agreed that exports were unlikely to be affected significantly.

He said that the only export pipeline route with any spare capacity was the Druzhba system passing through Ukraine, where prohibitively high Ukrainian transport tariffs would mean Russian exports through it were unlikely to rise.
Stephen O'Sullivan, director of oil and gas research at MC Securities in London, said Druzhba exports could also be capped by the lack of demand at the other end.
"Druzhba is the only pipeline with spare capacity, but the question is do Central European countries want any more oil from it?" he said. "They now have alternative supply sources."
O'Sullivan said that the other two main export routes -- to Novorossiisk in the Black Sea and Ventspils on the Baltic Sea -- were full to overflowing.
Tariffs along the sprawling system are charged on a per kilometre basis and average around 20 roubles per tonne.
Analysts said transportation costs varied widely, according to where a company's production base was situated, but added that they represent a big slice of output and marketing costs.
Domestic producers and foreign oil companies operating in Russia have frequently attacked Transneft, the state-owned oil pipeline monopoly, for charging too much.
The crude system stretches for 50,000 km (31,000 miles), with product pipelines covering 20,500 km (12,700 miles).
Some traders and analysts said the FEC's role in Russia's energy sector was still unclear, casting doubt over whether the body had the political clout to push through tariff cuts.

"It is difficult to know the exact role of the FEC, so I would side with those who are slightly sceptical (of the tariff cut announcement)," Martin Cocker, director of Ernst and Young's CIS energy group in Moscow, said.
The FEC was the brain-child of first deputy premier Anatoly Chubais, set up to inject market economy principles into the energy sector.

One Moscow-based oil trader said the FEC's move may have been timed to coincide with a power vacuum at the top of the oil industry. Pyotr Rodionov resigned from his post of Fuel and Energy Minister earlier this month and has yet to be replaced.

"When there is no oil minister, then this is a time when people tend to throw in a new proposal for maximum impact," the trader said. "Announcing something and implementing it are two very different things."
But with the backing of the powerful Russian oil lobby, others said tariff cuts were likely soon.
O'Sullivan said that the move to cut oil transport tariffs was part of Russia's overall drive to restructure natural monopolies like gas, electricity and railroads.

In total Russia, the world's third largest oil producer, exported 105 million tonnes of crude (2.1 million barrels per day) outside the Commonwealth of Independent States last year, despite a slight decline in production.
Non-CIS oil product exports also rose, to 55 million tonnes (1.1 million bpd) in 1996 from 44 million (800,000 bpd) in 1995.
($1=5,751 roubles)
